title: Weighted picks
summary: Make cherries common and sevens rare: three algorithms, three speeds.

cards.title: Not all symbols are equal
cards.body: A game designer says: cherries 40%, lemons 30%, bells 20%, sevens 10%. Write those as **weights** `40, 30, 20, 10`. Draw a fair random number from 0 to 99 and turn it into a symbol. Three ways to do it:

cards.title: 1. Linear scan: O(n)
cards.body: Lay the weights end to end like slices of a ruler. Walk along, subtracting, until r lands inside a slice.

cards.title: 2. Running totals + binary search: O(log n)
cards.body: Store the running totals once. Then each pick is a binary search: the first total greater than r. This is **prefix sums** and **binary search** from the Foundations track, working together.

cards.title: 3. The alias method: O(1)
cards.body: Vose's alias method pre-builds a table where every column has height exactly 1. A pick is then one uniform column plus one biased coin, however many symbols there are.

cards.title: Which one should a game use?
cards.body:
- A handful of symbols: linear is perfectly fine and the easiest to audit.
- Hundreds of entries (big virtual reels, prize tables): running totals + binary search.
- Millions of picks per second over a fixed table (simulations): the alias method.

All three give **exactly the same probabilities**. The tests in this app check that for random weight tables.

cards.question: Weights `40, 30, 20, 10`, running totals `40, 70, 90, 100`. Which symbol does r = 70 pick?
cards.explain: The first running total GREATER than 70 is 90, at index 2. (r = 69 would still be index 1.)

cards.title: Build it: a weighted reel
cards.body: Write `runningTotals` and a binary-search `pickWeighted`. The tests check every single value of r maps to the right symbol.
